turns.say: へやを そうじしましょうか。
turns.en: Shall I help you clean the room?
turns.cue: Ask her to open the window.
accept: まどを あけてください
turns.tip: The te-form plus ください is a polite request.
slips: あけるください
ください follows the te-form: あけて.

turns.say: はい、あけます。でんきは。
turns.cue: Ask her to turn it off.
accept: でんきを けしてください
turns.tip: けす covers turning off and rubbing out.
slips: けしますください
The request is けして ください.

turns.say: けしました。
turns.cue: Ask whether you may sit down.
accept: すわってもいいですか
turns.tip: 〜てもいいですか asks for permission.
slips: すわりますか
That asks whether you sit, not whether you may.

turns.say: もちろん。どうぞ。
turns.cue: Ask her to help you.
accept: てつだってください
turns.tip: てつだう becomes てつだって in the te-form.
slips: てつだいてください
う-verbs ending in う take って: てつだって.

turns.say: いいですよ。なにを しますか。
turns.en: Happy to. What shall I do?
turns.cue: Say you will wash this and then go out.
accept: これを あらって、でかけます
turns.tip: The te-form strings actions together in order.
slips: あらいます、でかけます
Link them with the te-form: あらって.

turns.say: いそぎましょうか。
turns.cue: Ask her to take her time.
accept: ゆっくりしてください
ゆっくりでいいです
turns.tip: ゆっくり is the everyday way of saying "no rush".
slips: いそいでください
That asks her to hurry — the opposite.

lessons.title: Family Picture
lessons.sub: Things in progress, describing people, joining sentences
lessons.kanji: 人先生学校友父母男女子

drills.q: Say you are eating right now.
drills.a: いま ごはんを たべています
w: いま ごはんを たべます
That is the plain present, which covers habits and the future.
いま ごはんを たべてます です
です does not follow a verb like this.
いま ごはんを たべるています
ている attaches to the te-form: たべて.
drills.why: te-form plus いる is the present continuous.

drills.q: Say your older brother is married.
drills.a: あには けっこんしています
w: あには けっこんします
That means he is going to get married.
あには けっこんしました
That reports the wedding as an event, not his current state.
あには けっこんです
けっこん needs する to work as a verb.
drills.why: With verbs of change, ている describes the state that resulted. It is "is married", not "is getting married".

drills.q: Say Mary has long hair.
drills.a: メアリーさんは かみが ながいです
w: メアリーさんの かみは ながいです が
The trailing が leaves it hanging.
メアリーさんは かみを ながいです
The feature takes が, not を.
メアリーさんは ながい かみが います
います is for living things existing.
drills.why: The person is the topic with は and the feature takes が: 〜は 〜が [adjective].

drills.q: Say this restaurant is cheap and tasty.
drills.a: この みせは やすくて おいしいです
w: この みせは やすいで おいしいです
い-adjectives take くて, not で.
この みせは やすくて おいしいでした
That puts it in the past.
この みせは やすいと おいしいです
と joins nouns, not adjectives.
drills.why: い-adjectives join with くて; な-adjectives and nouns join with で.

drills.q: Say you are going to see a film.
drills.a: えいがを みに いきます
w: えいがを みるに いきます
The pattern uses the ます-stem: み.
えいがを みてに いきます
The te-form does not go before に here.
えいがを みに います
います means "exist", not "go".
drills.why: Stem plus に plus a motion verb means going in order to do something.

grammar.b: te-form plus いる is the present continuous: happening right now. In casual speech the い disappears — たべてる.
e: いま ごはんを たべています。
I am eating right now.
なにを していますか。
What are you doing?

grammar.t: 〜ている for a state that resulted
grammar.b: The same form also describes a state left behind by a past change, which English handles with a plain present. けっこんしています means "is married", not "is getting married". It covers しっています (know), すんでいます (live), つとめています (work for).
e: あには けっこんしています。
My older brother is married.
ナナイモに すんでいます。
I live in Nanaimo.

grammar.b: To describe a part of someone, name the part with が and then the adjective: かみが ながいです. The person is the topic with は, the feature takes が.
e: メアリーさんは かみが ながいです。
Mary has long hair.
たけしさんは せが たかいです。
Takeshi is tall.

grammar.b: Adjectives and nouns have te-forms too, for joining descriptions. い-adjectives swap い for くて (やすくて), な-adjectives and nouns take で (しずかで, がくせいで).
e: この みせは やすくて おいしいです。
This restaurant is cheap and tasty.
しずかで きれいな まちです。
It is a quiet, pretty town.

grammar.b: Take the ます-stem, add に, then a motion verb: "go in order to do". たべに いきます is "go to eat".
e: えいがを みに いきます。
I am going to see a film.
ひるごはんを たべに かえります。
I am going home to eat lunch.

grammar.b: ひとり and ふたり are irregular; from three on it is the number plus にん — さんにん, よにん (not よんにん), ごにん.
e: かぞくは よにんです。
There are four people in my family.
ともだちが ふたり きました。
Two friends came.

vocab: to work for, to be employed

scene.title: The family photo
scene.role: Kaku is a friend looking at your photos
scene.setting: She has picked up a picture of your family.

turns.say: これは かぞくの しゃしんですか。
turns.en: Is this a photo of your family?
turns.cue: Say yes, it is your family.
accept: はい、かぞくです
はい、わたしの かぞくです
turns.tip: の links the two nouns: わたしの かぞく.

turns.say: おねえさんは どの ひとですか。
turns.en: Which one is your older sister?
turns.cue: Say she is the one with long hair.
accept: かみが ながい ひとです
かみが ながいです
turns.tip: The feature takes が: かみが ながい.
slips: かみは ながい
A feature of someone takes が, not は.

turns.say: おにいさんは なにを していますか。
turns.en: What does your older brother do?
turns.cue: Say he works for a bank.
accept: ぎんこうに つとめています
turns.tip: つとめる takes に for the employer, and ている for a standing state.
slips: ぎんこうで つとめています
つとめる takes に: ぎんこうに.
つとめます
A job you hold now is つとめています.

turns.say: けっこんして いますか。
turns.cue: Say yes, he is married.
accept: はい、けっこんしています
turns.tip: Married is a resulting state, so ている, never けっこんします.
slips: けっこんします
That means he is going to get married.

turns.say: どこに すんで いますか。
turns.cue: Say he lives in Tokyo.
accept: とうきょうに すんでいます
turns.tip: すむ always comes with ている when you mean "lives there".
slips: すみます
Where someone lives is すんでいます.
とうきょうで すんで
すむ takes に.

turns.say: おとうとさんは。
turns.cue: Say he is a high school student.
accept: おとうとは こうこうの がくせいです
こうこうの がくせいです
turns.tip: Your own family takes the plain words: おとうと, not おとうとさん.
slips: おとうとさんは
さん-words are for someone else’s family.

lessons.title: Barbecue
lessons.sub: Casual speech, reporting what people say and think

drills.q: Which is the short negative of いく?
drills.a: いかない
w: いきない
う-verbs change the final sound to あ: いか.
いくない
The final う has to change before ない.
いけない
That is the potential form turning negative.
drills.why: う-verbs take the あ row before ない, except う endings which become わ.

drills.q: Say you think it will rain tomorrow.
drills.a: あした あめが ふると おもいます
w: あした あめが ふりますと おもいます
The quoted part goes in short form.
あした あめが ふると おもます
おもう becomes おもいます.
あした あめが ふるを おもいます
と is the quotation marker here, not を.
drills.why: Put the thought in short form, then と, then 思います.

drills.q: Report that Takeshi said he was busy.
drills.a: たけしさんは いそがしいと いっていました
w: たけしさんは いそがしいと いいました
For reporting what someone said, いっていました is the natural form.
たけしさんは いそがしいですと いっていました
The quoted part takes the short form.
たけしさんが いそがしいと いっていました
The speaker is the topic, so は.
drills.why: Mark the speaker with は, quote in short form, and finish with といっていました.

drills.q: Ask someone not to take photographs.
drills.a: しゃしんを とらないでください
w: しゃしんを とらなくてください
The pattern is ないで, not なくて.
しゃしんを とりませんでください
It attaches to the short negative: とらない.
しゃしんを とらないください
で is needed between ない and ください.
drills.why: Take the short negative, drop the い, and add でください.

drills.q: Say you like reading books.
drills.a: ほんを よむのが すきです
w: ほんを よむが すきです
The verb needs の to become a noun first.
ほんを よみますのが すきです
の attaches to the short form.
ほんを よむのを すきです
すき takes が.
drills.why: の turns the verb into a noun, and すき marks what is liked with が.

grammar.b: The dictionary form is the short present: たべる, のむ, いく. The negative drops ます and uses ない: たべない, のまない, いかない. For う-verbs the final sound becomes あ, except う-endings which become わ — かう → かわない. する → しない, くる → こない, ある → ない.
e: たべる / たべない
eat / do not eat
いく / いかない
go / do not go

grammar.b: Short forms are how friends and family talk. Use them down the social ladder or sideways to people you know well, and keep ます for teachers, strangers and anyone at work. Getting this wrong sounds rude rather than friendly.
e: あした なにを する？
What are you doing tomorrow?
べんきょうする。
I'm going to study.

grammar.b: To say what you think, put the thought in short form, then と思います. The と is the quotation marker — everything before it is the thought.
e: あした あめが ふると おもいます。
I think it will rain tomorrow.
たかいと おもいます。
I think it is expensive.

grammar.b: The same structure reports what someone said. Mark the speaker with は, quote in short form, finish with といっていました.
e: たけしさんは いそがしいと いっていました。
Takeshi said he was busy.
あした くると いっていました。
He said he will come tomorrow.

grammar.b: The negative request: please do not. Take the short negative, drop the い, add でください.
e: わすれないでください。
Please do not forget.
しゃしんを とらないでください。
Please do not take photographs.

grammar.b: To like doing something, turn the verb into a noun with の, then mark it with が. The same trick works with じょうず (good at) and へた (bad at).
e: ほんを よむのが すきです。
I like reading books.
りょうりを するのが じょうずです。
He is good at cooking.

grammar.t: なにか and なにも
grammar.b: なにか means "something" and takes no particle. なにも means "nothing" and needs a negative verb. The same split runs through だれか／だれも and どこか／どこも.
e: なにか たべましたか。
Did you eat something?
なにも たべませんでした。
I ate nothing.

vocab: to rest, to take time off

scene.title: The barbecue
scene.role: Kaku is a friend, speaking casually
scene.setting: Sorting out tomorrow, in the short forms friends use.

turns.say: あしたの パーティー、くる。
turns.cue: Say you think you will go.
accept: いくと おもいます
turns.tip: 〜と思います takes the short form in front of it.
slips: いきますと おもいます
The short form goes before と: いくと.

turns.say: りょうりは じょうず。
turns.en: Are you any good at cooking?
turns.cue: Say you are bad at cooking.
accept: りょうりは へたです
へたです
turns.tip: じょうず and へた are both な-adjectives.
slips: へたいです
へた takes です on its own.

turns.say: だれが りょうりを する。
turns.cue: Say Tanaka said he would do it.
accept: たなかさんが すると いっていました
turns.tip: Reporting what someone said is 〜と言っていました.
slips: いいました
〜と言っていました is the usual way to report it.

turns.say: にわで たべる。
turns.en: Shall we eat in the garden?
turns.cue: Say you think it will probably rain.
accept: たぶん あめが ふると おもいます
turns.tip: たぶん and 〜と思います go together naturally.
slips: ふりますと
Short form before と: ふると.

turns.say: じゃあ、うちで しよう。
turns.cue: Say you like eating at home.
accept: うちで たべるのが すきです
turns.tip: のが turns the verb into the thing you like.
slips: たべますのが
The short form takes の: たべるのが.

turns.say: なにか かう。
turns.cue: Ask her not to buy anything.
accept: なにも かわないでください
turns.tip: なにも needs the negative after it.
slips: なにか かわないで
With a negative it becomes なにも.

lessons.title: Kabuki
lessons.sub: The past in short form, and describing nouns with whole sentences

drills.q: Which is the past short form of たべる?
drills.a: たべた
w: たべった
る-verbs simply swap て for た: たべて, たべた.
たべました
That is the polite past, not the short form.
たべなかった
That is the past negative.
drills.why: Take the te-form and change て to た. Every te-form you know converts for free.

drills.q: Say the film you saw yesterday was interesting.
drills.a: きのう みた えいがは おもしろかったです
w: きのう みました えいがは おもしろかったです
The verb in front of a noun takes the short form.
えいがは きのう みたが おもしろかったです
The description goes in front of the noun it describes.
きのう みた えいがは おもしろいでした
い-adjectives do not take でした.
drills.why: Japanese puts the whole description before the noun, with no word for "that" or "which".

drills.q: Say you have not eaten yet.
drills.a: まだ たべていません
w: まだ たべませんでした
That is a flat past negative, not "not yet".
もう たべていません
もう with a negative means "not any more".
まだ たべません
The pattern needs ていません.
drills.why: "Not yet" is まだ plus ていません, even though English uses a past tense here.

drills.q: Say you have already eaten lunch.
drills.a: もう ひるごはんを たべました
w: まだ ひるごはんを たべました
まだ means "still" or "not yet".
もう ひるごはんを たべます
もう with "already" needs the past.
もう ひるごはんを たべています
That says you are in the middle of eating.
drills.why: もう plus the past means "already".

drills.q: Say it was cold, so you stayed home (casually, to a friend).
drills.a: さむかったから、うちに いた
w: さむいでしたから、うちに いた
い-adjectives do not take でした.
うちに いたから、さむかった
That reverses cause and effect.
さむかったですから、うちに いた
Mixing polite です with the casual いた is inconsistent.
drills.why: In casual speech both halves stay in short form, with から after the reason.

grammar.b: The past short form is the te-form with て swapped for た: たべて → たべた, のんで → のんだ, いって → いった. The negative replaces ない with なかった: たべなかった. Because it follows the te-form, every te-form you already know converts for free.
e: たべた / たべなかった
ate / did not eat
いった / いかなかった
went / did not go

grammar.b: Slot the past short form into the same と思います and と言っていました frames from Lesson 8. Only the quoted part changes tense; the frame stays in the present.
e: もう たべたと おもいます。
I think he has already eaten.
おもしろかったと いっていました。
She said it was interesting.

grammar.t: Describing nouns with a whole clause
grammar.b: Japanese puts the description in front of the noun, however long it is: きのう みた えいが is "the film I saw yesterday". The verb inside goes in short form, and there is no relative pronoun — no "that" or "which".
e: きのう みた えいがは おもしろかったです。
The film I saw yesterday was interesting.
ははが つくった りょうりが すきです。
I like the food my mother made.

grammar.b: もう + past means "already". まだ + 〜ていません means "not yet" — note that English uses a past tense here and Japanese does not. まだ with a positive verb means "still".
e: もう ひるごはんを たべました。
I have already eaten lunch.
まだ たべていません。
I have not eaten yet.

grammar.b: から joins reason to result just as in Lesson 6, but in casual speech the reason sits in short form: さむいから, いかないから.
e: さむいから、うちに いた。
It was cold, so I stayed home.
あしたは しけんが あるから、べんきょうします。
I have a test tomorrow, so I will study.

scene.title: After the kabuki
scene.role: Kaku is the friend you went with

turns.say: かぶきは どうでしたか。
turns.cue: Say it was interesting.
accept: おもしろかったです
turns.tip: An い-adjective goes to 〜かった in the past.
slips: おもしろいでした
い-adjectives change themselves: おもしろかったです.

turns.say: きっぷは たかかった。
turns.cue: Say they were expensive.
accept: たかかったです
きっぷは たかかったです
turns.tip: Same change: たかい becomes たかかった.
slips: たかいでした
たかかったです.

turns.say: しゅくだいは もう しましたか。
turns.en: Have you done the homework yet?
turns.cue: Say not yet.
accept: まだです
まだ していません
turns.tip: まだ answers もう, and takes a negative when you spell it out.
slips: まだ しました
まだ needs the negative: まだ していません.

turns.say: しけんは いつですか。
turns.cue: Say it begins tomorrow.
accept: あした はじまります
turns.tip: はじまる is something that begins by itself.

turns.say: つかれましたか。
turns.cue: Say you walked a lot, so you are tired.
accept: たくさん あるきましたから、つかれました
turns.tip: から comes after the reason, not before it.
slips: から たくさん あるきました
The reason comes first, then から.

turns.say: はじめて かぶきを みましたか。
turns.cue: Say it was the first time.
accept: はじめてでした
はじめて みました
turns.tip: はじめて covers "for the first time" on its own.

lessons.title: Winter Vacation Plans
lessons.sub: Comparing things, intentions, and change

drills.q: Say the train is faster than the bus.
drills.a: でんしゃの ほうが バスより はやいです
w: でんしゃより バスの ほうが はやいです
That says the bus is faster.
でんしゃの ほうが バスより はやくです
The adjective takes です as it is.
でんしゃが バスの ほうが はやいです
The thing that wins takes のほうが.
drills.why: A の ほうが B より means A is more. Reversing the two swaps the meaning.

drills.q: Ask which fruit they like best.
drills.a: くだもので なにが いちばん すきですか
w: くだものが なにが いちばん すきですか
The group takes で.
くだもので なにが もっと すきですか
もっと is "more", not "most".
くだもので だれが いちばん すきですか
だれ asks about people.
drills.why: Within a group, use [group]で なにが いちばん.

drills.q: Say you intend to go to Japan in the summer.
drills.a: なつやすみに にほんに いくつもりです
w: なつやすみに にほんに いきますつもりです
つもり follows the short form.
なつやすみに にほんに いくつもります
つもり is a noun and takes です.
なつやすみに にほんに いって つもりです
The te-form does not go before つもり.
drills.why: Short form plus つもりです states a decision you have already made.

drills.q: Say it has got cold.
drills.a: さむく なりました
w: さむい なりました
い-adjectives change to く before なる.
さむに なりました
に is for な-adjectives and nouns.
さむく なりました です
ました already closes the sentence.
drills.why: い-adjectives take く before なる; な-adjectives and nouns take に.

drills.q: Say you go to school by train.
drills.a: でんしゃで がっこうに いきます
w: でんしゃに がっこうに いきます
に is the destination, and you cannot have two.
でんしゃを がっこうに いきます
The means of transport takes で.
でんしゃで がっこうで いきます
The destination takes に.
drills.why: で covers the means as well as the place. Walking is the exception: あるいて.

grammar.b: AのほうがBより + adjective says A is more... than B. You can flip it to BよりAのほうが with no change in meaning. In an answer, のほうが alone is enough.
e: でんしゃの ほうが バスより はやいです。
The train is faster than the bus.
なつの ほうが すきです。
I prefer summer.

grammar.b: With a whole group, use [group]でいちばん + adjective. The group can be a category (くだもので), a place (にほんで) or a list.
e: くだもので なにが いちばん すきですか。
Which fruit do you like best?
りんごが いちばん すきです。
I like apples best.

grammar.t: の standing in for a noun
grammar.b: Once the noun is obvious, replace it with の: あかいの is "the red one". This is the same の you met in 〜のが好きです, doing the same job.
e: もっと やすいのが ありますか。
Do you have a cheaper one?
おおきいのを ください。
The big one, please.

grammar.b: Short form plus つもりです states a firm intention — something you have decided, not a vague hope.
e: なつやすみに にほんに いくつもりです。
I intend to go to Japan in the summer.
かいものは しないつもりです。
I do not plan to go shopping.

grammar.b: なる means "become". い-adjectives change their ending to く (さむくなる), な-adjectives and nouns take に (げんきになる, せんせいになる).
e: さむく なりました。
It has got cold.
にほんごが じょうずに なりました。
My Japanese has got better.

grammar.t: どこかに and どこにも
grammar.b: どこかに means "(to) somewhere", どこにも with a negative means "(to) nowhere". Matching pairs exist for なにか／なにも and だれか／だれも.
e: なつやすみに どこかに いきましたか。
Did you go anywhere in the summer?
どこにも いきませんでした。
I did not go anywhere.

grammar.b: The same で that marks where an action happens also marks what you do it by: train, bus, bike. On foot is the exception — あるいて, the te-form of あるく.
e: でんしゃで がっこうに いきます。
I go to school by train.
あるいて かえりました。
I walked home.

scene.title: Winter plans
scene.role: Kaku is a friend comparing plans with you
scene.setting: Last class before the winter break.

turns.say: ふゆやすみは なにを する つもりですか。
turns.en: What do you intend to do over the winter break?
turns.cue: Say you intend to go to Japan.
accept: にほんへ いく つもりです
にほんに いく つもりです
turns.tip: つもり follows the short form: いく つもり.
slips: いきます つもり
Short form before つもり: いく つもりです.

turns.say: でんしゃと ひこうき、どちらが はやいですか。
turns.en: Which is faster, the train or the plane?
turns.cue: Say the plane is faster.
accept: ひこうきの ほうが はやいです
turns.tip: The winner takes のほうが.
slips: ひこうきが はやいより
より marks the one you beat, not the winner.

turns.say: でも、でんしゃの ほうが やすいですよ。
turns.cue: Ask whether the train is convenient.
accept: でんしゃは べんりですか
turns.tip: べんり is a な-adjective, so it takes です plainly.
slips: べんりいですか
べんり takes です directly.

turns.say: はい、べんりです。
turns.cue: Say it gets cold in winter.
accept: ふゆは さむく なります
turns.tip: An い-adjective drops い and takes く before なる.
slips: さむい なります
さむい becomes さむく before なります.

turns.say: きせつの なかで どれが いちばん すきですか。
turns.en: Which season do you like best?
turns.cue: Say you like spring best.
accept: はるが いちばん すきです
turns.tip: いちばん does the work of "the most".
slips: はるは いちばん
The thing picked out of a group takes が.

turns.say: ひとりで いきますか。
turns.en: Are you going on your own?
turns.cue: Say you will go with a friend.
accept: ともだちと いきます
turns.tip: と again for company.
slips: ともだちで
で is not for company; と is.

lessons.title: After the Vacation
lessons.sub: What you want to do, listing activities, and experience

drills.q: Say you want to go to Japan.
drills.a: にほんに いきたいです
w: にほんに いくたいです
たい attaches to the ます-stem: いき.
にほんに いきたいます
たい behaves like an い-adjective, so です.
にほんに いきたいでした
The past would be いきたかったです.
drills.why: Swap ます for たい. The result conjugates like an い-adjective.

drills.q: Say that on Sunday you read and watched films, among other things.
drills.a: にちようびは ほんを よんだり、えいがを みたり しました
w: にちようびは ほんを よんで、えいがを みて しました
The te-form lists actions in order, not as samples.
にちようびは ほんを よみたり、えいがを みたり しました
たり attaches to the past short form: よんだ.
にちようびは ほんを よんだり、えいがを みたり います
The pattern ends with する.
drills.why: Past short form plus り, repeated, then する. It means "among other things".

drills.q: Say you have never eaten sushi.
drills.a: すしを たべたことが ありません
w: すしを たべることが ありません
Experience uses the past short form: たべた.
すしを たべたことが いません
こと is not alive, so あります.
すしを たべませんでした
That is simply "I did not eat it", about one occasion.
drills.why: Past short form plus ことがある is about life experience, not about the past itself.

drills.q: Say you bought books, magazines and so on.
drills.a: ほんや ざっしを かいました
w: ほんと ざっしを かいました
と gives a complete list with nothing left out.
ほんや ざっしや かいました
The last item still needs its own particle, here を.
ほんも ざっしを かいました
も means "too", which is a different idea.
drills.why: や lists examples and suggests there were others; と is exhaustive.

grammar.b: Swap ます for たい to say you want to do something. The result behaves like an い-adjective: たべたいです, たべたくないです, たべたかったです. The object can take が instead of を.
e: にほんに いきたいです。
I want to go to Japan.
なにも たべたくないです。
I do not want to eat anything.

grammar.b: To give a sample of what you did rather than a complete list, take past short forms, add り, and finish with する in the tense you need. The implication is "among other things".
e: にちようびは ほんを よんだり、えいがを みたり しました。
On Sunday I read and watched films, among other things.
うちで そうじしたり せんたくしたり します。
At home I clean, do laundry and so on.

grammar.b: Past short form plus ことがあります says you have done something at least once in your life. It is about experience, not about the past as such, so it does not work for yesterday.
e: にほんに いったことが あります。
I have been to Japan.
すしを たべたことが ありません。
I have never eaten sushi.

grammar.b: や lists examples rather than everything, unlike と which is exhaustive. Often followed by など, "and so on".
e: ほんや ざっしを かいました。
I bought books, magazines and so on.
やさいや くだものが すきです。
I like vegetables, fruit and the like.

scene.title: Back from the break
scene.role: Kaku is a friend catching up with you

turns.say: やすみは なにを しましたか。
turns.en: What did you do over the break?
turns.cue: Say you did things like a part-time job and studying.
accept: アルバイトを したり、べんきょうしたり しました
turns.tip: 〜たり〜たり lists a couple of things out of many.
slips: アルバイトと べんきょうを しました
For a sample of what you did, 〜たり〜たり.

turns.say: おんせんに いった ことが ありますか。
turns.en: Have you ever been to a hot spring?
turns.cue: Say you never have.
accept: ありません
いった ことが ありません
turns.tip: 〜ことがある is about experience, ever, in a lifetime.
slips: いきませんでした
That is about one past occasion, not ever.

turns.say: いきたいですか。
turns.cue: Say you want to go.
accept: はい、いきたいです
いきたいです
turns.tip: 〜たい comes off the ます-stem: いき + たい.
slips: いくたいです
From the stem: いきたい.

turns.say: しろも みたいですか。
turns.en: Do you want to see a castle too?
turns.cue: Say you want to see castles and so on.
accept: しろなどを みたいです
しろが みたいです
turns.tip: など rounds a list off, like "and so on".

turns.say: おかねは だいじょうぶですか。
turns.en: Are you all right for money?
turns.cue: Say you are looking for a part-time job.
accept: アルバイトを さがしています
turns.tip: Something you are in the middle of takes ている.
slips: さがします
In progress now: さがしています.

turns.say: いい おもいでに なりますよ。
turns.cue: Say you are happy.
accept: うれしいです
turns.tip: うれしい is how you feel now, not a general trait.
slips: たのしいです
たのしい describes the thing; うれしい is you.

lessons.title: Feeling Ill
lessons.sub: Explaining, overdoing, advice and obligation

drills.q: The doctor asks what is wrong. Explain that you have a headache.
drills.a: あたまが いたいんです
w: あたまが いたいです
Correct Japanese, but it states a fact rather than explaining your situation.
あたまが いたいなんです
な is only needed after な-adjectives and nouns.
あたまを いたいんです
The part that hurts takes が.
drills.why: んです frames what you say as the explanation behind the situation, which is what the question invites.

drills.q: Say you ate too much last night.
drills.a: ゆうべ たべすぎました
w: ゆうべ たべるすぎました
すぎる attaches to the stem: たべ.
ゆうべ たべすぎでした
すぎる is a verb, so たべすぎました.
ゆうべ たくさん たべすぎます
That puts it in the present.
drills.why: Add すぎる to a verb stem or an adjective root for doing something to excess.

drills.q: Advise someone to take some medicine.
drills.a: くすりを のんだほうが いいです
w: くすりを のむほうが いいです
This pattern uses the past short form, のんだ.
くすりを のまないほうが いいです
That advises against taking it.
くすりを のんだほうが いいます
いい is an adjective and takes です.
drills.why: Past short form plus ほうがいいです gives advice. The past form here has nothing to do with past time.

drills.q: Say you have to take medicine.
drills.a: くすりを のまなければ いけません
w: くすりを のまなければ いけます
The set phrase is いけません.
くすりを のまないければ いけません
Drop the い from のまない before ければ.
くすりを のまなくても いいです
That says you do not have to.
drills.why: Take the short negative, drop い, add ければいけません. In speech it contracts to のまなきゃ.

drills.q: Say you have a fever, so you will take the day off.
drills.a: ねつが あるので、やすみます
w: ねつが あるですので、やすみます
ので attaches straight to the short form.
ねつが あるので、やすみました
That puts the result in the past.
ねつが ありますので、やすみます
Grammatical, but the short form before ので is the normal pattern here.
drills.why: ので is a softer, slightly more formal "because" than から.

grammar.b: Short form plus んです frames a statement as an explanation of the situation — giving a reason, asking for one, or softening a request. な-adjectives and nouns need な before it: しずかなんです, がくせいなんです.
e: あたまが いたいんです。
The thing is, I have a headache.
どうしたんですか。
What happened?

grammar.b: Add すぎる to a verb stem or an adjective root for "too much". たべすぎる is to overeat, たかすぎる is too expensive. It conjugates as a る-verb.
e: ゆうべ たべすぎました。
I ate too much last night.
この くつは たかすぎます。
These shoes are too expensive.

grammar.b: Advice. Use the past short form for "you should" (ねたほうがいいです) and the negative short form for "you should not" (いかないほうがいいです). The past form here has nothing to do with past time.
e: くすりを のんだほうが いいです。
You should take some medicine.
むりを しないほうが いいです。
You should not overdo it.

grammar.b: Another "because", a shade softer and more formal than から. It attaches to short forms, with な after な-adjectives and nouns.
e: ねつが あるので、やすみます。
I have a fever, so I will take the day off.
あめなので、いきません。
It is raining, so I will not go.

grammar.b: Obligation: "must". Take the short negative, drop い, add ければいけません. The casual contraction なきゃ is everywhere in speech — べんきょうしなきゃ.
e: くすりを のまなければ いけません。
I have to take medicine.
あした はやく おきなきゃ。
I have to get up early tomorrow.

grammar.b: Softens a question, adding a note of "I wonder". Useful when asking something you are not sure the other person can answer.
e: あめが ふるでしょうか。
I wonder if it will rain.
これで いいでしょうか。
Would this be all right?

scene.title: Feeling ill
scene.role: Kaku is a friend who can see you are not well
scene.setting: You have turned up looking rough.

turns.say: げんきが ないですね。どうしたんですか。
turns.en: You don't look well. What's the matter?
turns.cue: Say you have caught a cold.
accept: かぜを ひいたんです
かぜを ひきました
turns.tip: かぜ is caught with ひく, and んです explains a situation.
slips: かぜが あります
A cold is caught: かぜを ひきました.

turns.say: ねつが ありますか。
turns.cue: Say you have a fever and your throat hurts.
accept: ねつが あって、のどが いたいです
turns.tip: The te-form joins the two complaints.
slips: ねつが あります、のどが
Join them with the te-form: あって.

turns.say: ゆうべ なにを したんですか。
turns.en: What were you doing last night?
turns.cue: Say you studied too much.
accept: べんきょうしすぎました
turns.tip: 〜すぎる comes off the stem and means too much of it.
slips: べんきょうしました すぎ
Straight onto the stem: べんきょうしすぎました.

turns.say: むりは よくないですよ。
turns.cue: Say you have to go to class.
accept: じゅぎょうに いかなければいけません
turns.tip: Obligation is 〜なければいけません, off the ない-form.
slips: いきなければ
From the ない-form: いかなければ.

turns.say: やすんだ ほうが いいですよ。
turns.cue: Say you will take today off.
accept: きょうは やすみます
turns.tip: やすむ covers resting and taking the day off both.

turns.say: くすりを のんで、ねてください。
turns.en: Take some medicine and get some sleep.
turns.cue: Thank her and say you will be careful.
accept: ありがとうございます。きを つけます
turns.tip: きをつける is the everyday "I’ll be careful".

lessons.title: Looking for a Part-time Job
lessons.sub: What you can do, giving reasons, how things look

drills.q: Say you can speak Japanese.
drills.a: にほんごが はなせます
w: にほんごを はなせます
With potential verbs the object usually shifts to が.
にほんごが はなすできます
The potential of はなす is はなせる.
にほんごが はなせるます
はなせる is a る-verb: はなせます.
drills.why: う-verbs change the final u to e and add る: はなす to はなせる.

drills.q: Say it is cheap, and tasty too.
drills.a: やすいし、おいしいです
w: やすくて、おいしいです
Correct, but て simply joins. し stacks up reasons.
やすいですし、おいしい
The polite ending belongs at the end of the sentence.
やすいしと、おいしいです
し does not combine with と.
drills.why: し attaches to short forms and implies the list of reasons could go on.

drills.q: Say this cake looks delicious.
drills.a: この ケーキは おいしそうです
w: この ケーキは おいしいそうです
With い on the end it means "I hear it is delicious".
この ケーキは おいしみたいです
みたい is a different pattern, closer to "seems".
この ケーキは おいしそうます
そう takes です.
drills.why: Drop the い from the adjective and add そう for how something looks to you.

grammar.b: A separate conjugation for "can do". る-verbs take られる (たべられる), う-verbs change the final u to e plus る (よむ → よめる), する → できる, くる → こられる. The object usually shifts from を to が.
e: にほんごが はなせます。
I can speak Japanese.

grammar.b: Stacks up reasons: "and what is more". Attaches to short forms and implies the list could go on.
e: やすいし、おいしいです。
It is cheap, and tasty too.

grammar.b: Attached to an adjective root or verb stem, it reports how something looks to you right now. おいしそう is "looks delicious".
e: この ケーキは おいしそうです。
This cake looks delicious.

grammar.b: te-form plus みる means to try something and see how it goes.
e: きものを きてみました。
I tried wearing a kimono.

grammar.b: Picks up a topic someone else raised and comments on it: "if we are talking about X".
e: にほんごなら、たけしさんが じょうずです。
If it is Japanese you need, Takeshi is good at it.

grammar.b: Period に number + counter: いっしゅうかんに さんかい, three times a week.
e: いっしゅうかんに さんかい ジムに いきます。
I go to the gym three times a week.

lessons.title: Valentine's Day
lessons.sub: Wanting things, giving and receiving, suggestions

drills.q: Say you want a new car.
drills.a: あたらしい くるまが ほしいです
w: あたらしい くるまを ほしいです
ほしい is an adjective, so the thing wanted takes が.
あたらしい くるまが ほしいます
ほしい is an い-adjective and takes です.
あたらしい くるまが ほしたいです
たい is for verbs; ほしい is for things.
drills.why: ほしい wants a thing; 〜たい wants to do something.

drills.q: Say your friend gave you a present.
drills.a: ともだちが プレゼントを くれました
w: ともだちが プレゼントを あげました
あげる is giving away from you, not to you.
ともだちに プレゼントを くれました
The giver takes が.
ともだちが プレゼントを もらいました
もらう is from your side: you receive.
drills.why: くれる is the one that points at you. あげる points away, もらう is receiving.

drills.q: Say you only have a hundred yen.
drills.a: ひゃくえんしか ありません
w: ひゃくえんしか あります
しか always finishes with a negative.
ひゃくえんも ありません
も after a number means the amount is large.
ひゃくえんだけ ありません
だけ is neutral and does not need a negative.
drills.why: しか plus a negative means "only", with a sense of it not being enough.

grammar.b: "Want" for things rather than actions. It is an い-adjective and the thing wanted takes が.
e: あたらしい くるまが ほしいです。
I want a new car.

grammar.b: "Might". Weaker than でしょう, attaches to short forms.
e: あした あめが ふるかもしれません。
It might rain tomorrow.

grammar.t: あげる, くれる, もらう
grammar.b: Three verbs for giving, chosen by direction. あげる is giving away from me, くれる is someone giving to me, もらう is me receiving. Getting the direction wrong is the classic mistake here.
e: ともだちに プレゼントを あげました。
I gave my friend a present.

grammar.b: Suggesting a course of action to someone else: "why not...?".
e: びょういんに いったら どうですか。
Why not go to the hospital?

grammar.t: Number + も and しか + negative
grammar.b: も after a number says the amount is surprisingly large; しか with a negative verb says it is disappointingly small.
e: ひゃくえんしか ありません。
I only have a hundred yen.

lessons.title: A Trip to Nagano
lessons.sub: Intentions, preparation, and longer descriptions

drills.q: Say "let's eat lunch" to a friend, casually.
drills.a: ひるごはんを たべよう
w: ひるごはんを たべましょう
Correct, but that is the polite form.
ひるごはんを たべるよう
る-verbs drop る before よう.
ひるごはんを たべろう
That is not a form of たべる.
drills.why: る-verbs take よう and う-verbs change u to o plus う: のむ to のもう.

drills.q: Say you are thinking of going to Japan.
drills.a: にほんに いこうと おもっています
w: にほんに いくと おもっています
That means you think someone will go.
にほんに いこうと おもいます
With ています it sounds like a plan you have been turning over.
にほんに いくつもりと おもっています
つもり does not combine with と思う.
drills.why: Volitional plus と思っています is a plan you are weighing up.

drills.q: Say you will buy the tickets in advance.
drills.a: きっぷを かっておきます
w: きっぷを かってあります
てある describes a state someone has left behind.
きっぷを かっています
That says you are in the middle of buying them.
きっぷを かうておきます
おく attaches to the te-form: かって.
drills.why: ておく is doing something ahead of time, ready for later.

grammar.b: The casual "let's": る-verbs take よう (たべよう), う-verbs change u to o plus う (のむ → のもう), する → しよう, くる → こよう. It is the short-form counterpart of ましょう.
e: ひるごはんを たべよう。
Let's have lunch.

grammar.b: States a plan you have been turning over, slightly less fixed than つもり.
e: なつやすみに にほんに いこうと おもっています。
I am thinking of going to Japan in the summer.

grammar.b: Doing something in advance, in preparation. Contracts to 〜とく in speech.
e: きっぷを かっておきます。
I will buy the tickets in advance.

grammar.b: The Lesson 9 pattern stretched further: a whole clause in front of a noun, with the verb in short form.
e: わたしが とまった ホテルは きれいでした。
The hotel I stayed at was lovely.

lessons.title: Lost and Found
lessons.sub: Doing things for people, polite requests, and timing

drills.q: Say your friend helped you out.
drills.a: ともだちが てつだってくれました
w: ともだちが てつだってあげました
あげる points away from you.
ともだちに てつだってくれました
The person doing the favour takes が.
ともだちが てつだってもらいました
With もらう you would be the one receiving: ともだちに てつだってもらいました.
drills.why: てくれる is a favour coming towards you.

drills.q: Ask a stranger politely if they could help you.
drills.a: たすけていただけませんか
w: たすけてください
A plain request, too direct for a stranger.
たすけてもらいませんか
That is not the set polite form.
たすけていただきませんか
The polite request uses the potential: いただけ.
drills.why: ていただけませんか is the most polite of the request forms.

drills.q: Say that when you were a child, you swam a lot.
drills.a: こどものとき、よく およぎました
w: こどもとき、よく およぎました
A noun needs の before とき.
こどものとき、よく およぐました
およぐ becomes およぎます.
こどもだったとき、よく およぎました が
The trailing が leaves it hanging.
drills.why: Nouns take の before とき; verbs and adjectives take the short form.

grammar.t: 〜てあげる, 〜てくれる, 〜てもらう
grammar.b: The giving verbs applied to actions rather than objects: doing something for someone, someone doing it for me, getting someone to do it.
e: ともだちが てつだってくれました。
My friend helped me out.

grammar.b: The most polite way to ask for something. Use it with strangers and anyone senior to you.
e: たすけていただけませんか。
Could you please help me?

grammar.b: Expressing a hope: "it would be good if". With ですね it becomes a wish for the other person.
e: あめが やむと いいですね。
I hope the rain stops.

grammar.b: "When". The clause before とき is in short form, and its tense is relative to the main clause, not to now.
e: こどものとき、よく およぎました。
When I was a child I swam a lot.

grammar.b: Apologising for something specific you did.
e: おくれて すみませんでした。
I am sorry for being late.

lessons.title: Grumble and Gossip
lessons.sub: Hearsay, conditions, and what you need not do

drills.q: Say you hear Takeshi is going back to Japan.
drills.a: たけしさんは にほんに かえるそうです
w: たけしさんは にほんに かえりそうです
Attached to the stem it means "looks like he is about to".
たけしさんは にほんに かえるみたいです
みたい is your own impression, not something you were told.
たけしさんは にほんに かえるとです
と does not work on its own here.
drills.why: Short form plus そうです reports what you heard. Stem plus そう is how something looks.

drills.q: Say that if it rains, you will not go.
drills.a: あめが ふったら、いきません
w: あめが ふるたら、いきません
たら attaches to the past short form: ふった.
あめが ふりましたら、いきません
The short form is normal before たら.
あめが ふると、いきません
と is for automatic results, not for decisions.
drills.why: Past short form plus ら is the all-purpose "if" or "when".

drills.q: Say you do not have to come tomorrow.
drills.a: あした こなくてもいいです
w: あした こないでもいいです
The pattern uses なくて, not ないで.
あした こなければいけません
That says the opposite: you must come.
あした きなくてもいいです
くる becomes こない, so こなくて.
drills.why: Short negative, drop い, add くてもいいです.

grammar.b: Attached to a short form, this reports second-hand information. Note the contrast with Lesson 13: that one attaches to a stem and means "looks like".
e: たけしさんは にほんに かえるそうです。
I hear Takeshi is going back to Japan.

grammar.b: The casual version of と or そうです, very common in speech.
e: あした やすみだって。
Apparently tomorrow is a day off.

grammar.b: The all-purpose "if/when". Take the past short form and add ら.
e: あめが ふったら、いきません。
If it rains, I will not go.

grammar.b: "You do not have to". Take the short negative, drop い, add くてもいいです.
e: あした こなくてもいいです。
You do not have to come tomorrow.

grammar.b: "Seems like", based on your own impression. After nouns it works like a な-adjective.
e: かぜを ひいたみたいです。
It seems I have caught a cold.

grammar.b: Ordering events: 〜前に (before, with the dictionary form) and 〜てから (after, with the te-form).
e: ねる まえに はを みがきます。
I brush my teeth before bed.

lessons.title: John's Part-time Job
lessons.sub: Pairs of verbs, regret, and simultaneous actions

drills.q: Say the door opened (by itself).
drills.a: ドアが あきました
w: ドアを あけました
That says you opened it.
ドアが あけました
あける needs someone doing it, and takes を.
ドアを あきました
あく does not take an object.
drills.why: あく happens by itself and takes が; あける is done by someone and takes を.

drills.q: Say you went and lost your wallet.
drills.a: さいふを なくしてしまいました
w: さいふを なくしておきました
ておく is doing something deliberately in advance.
さいふを なくしました
Correct, but it loses the note of regret.
さいふを なくすてしまいました
しまう attaches to the te-form: なくして.
drills.why: てしまう adds either completion or regret. Here it is regret.

drills.q: Say you study while listening to music.
drills.a: おんがくを ききながら べんきょうします
w: おんがくを きくながら べんきょうします
ながら attaches to the ます-stem: きき.
おんがくを きいてながら べんきょうします
The te-form does not go before ながら.
べんきょうしながら おんがくを ききます
The main action goes last, so this swaps which one matters.
drills.why: Stem plus ながら, with the main activity in the second half.

grammar.b: Japanese has matched pairs: one verb for doing something to an object, another for the thing doing it itself. あける (I open it) against あく (it opens); おとす against おちる. The transitive one takes を.
e: ドアを あけました。 / ドアが あきました。
I opened the door. / The door opened.

grammar.b: With intransitive verbs, ている describes the state things are now in: まどが あいている, the window is open.
e: でんきが ついています。
The light is on.

grammar.b: Two senses: finishing something off, or doing something you regret. Contracts to 〜ちゃう in speech.
e: さいふを なくしてしまいました。
I went and lost my wallet.

grammar.b: "Whenever A, B follows". Used for natural consequences and instructions, not for one-off plans.
e: はるに なると、さくらが さきます。
When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

grammar.b: Two actions by one person at the same time. Attach ながら to the ます-stem; the main verb comes last.
e: おんがくを ききながら べんきょうします。
I study while listening to music.

grammar.b: Regret about something you did or did not do: "I should have".
e: もっと べんきょうすれば よかったです。
I should have studied more.

lessons.title: Meeting the Boss
lessons.sub: Honorific language and thanking people

drills.q: Ask your teacher politely what they will have to eat.
drills.a: せんせいは なにを めしあがりますか
w: せんせいは なにを たべますか
Polite, but it does not raise the other person.
せんせいは なにを いただきますか
いただく lowers you, so it is wrong for their action.
せんせいは なにを めしあがってですか
めしあがる conjugates normally: めしあがります.
drills.why: Honorific verbs raise the other person. めしあがる is the honorific of たべる and のむ.

drills.q: Thank a friend for helping you.
drills.a: てつだってくれて ありがとう
w: てつだってあげて ありがとう
あげる points away from you.
てつだうくれて ありがとう
It attaches to the te-form: てつだって.
てつだってもらって ありがとう
Possible, but てくれて is the natural way to thank someone.
drills.why: てくれて ありがとう thanks someone for a specific thing they did for you.

drills.q: Say you are glad you studied Japanese.
drills.a: にほんごを べんきょうして よかったです
w: にほんごを べんきょうして いいです
The set phrase is よかったです.
にほんごを べんきょうすると よかったです
That is a conditional, not a reflection.
にほんごを べんきょうしてよかったでした
よかった already carries the past.
drills.why: te-form plus よかったです expresses relief or satisfaction about something that turned out well.

grammar.b: Keigo raises the other person. Some verbs have special honorific forms — いらっしゃる for いる/いく/くる, めしあがる for たべる — and the rest use お + stem + になる.
e: せんせいは なにを めしあがりますか。
What will you have, sensei?

grammar.b: お + stem + ください is the polite imperative you hear in announcements and shops.
e: こちらに おかけください。
Please have a seat here.

grammar.b: Thanking someone for a specific action. The polite version is 〜てくださってありがとうございます.
e: てつだってくれて ありがとう。
Thanks for helping me.

grammar.b: Relief or satisfaction that something turned out well: "I am glad that...".
e: にほんごを べんきょうして よかったです。
I am glad I studied Japanese.

grammar.b: "Is supposed to" — what you expect on the basis of what you know.
e: たけしさんは もう ついたはずです。
Takeshi should have arrived by now.

vocab: to be, to go, to come (honorific)

lessons.title: Mary Goes Shopping
lessons.sub: Humble language and embedded questions

drills.q: Introduce yourself humbly as Yamada in a formal setting.
drills.a: やまだと もうします
w: やまだと いいます
Polite and fine day to day, but not the humble form.
やまだと おっしゃいます
おっしゃる raises the other person, so you cannot use it about yourself.
やまだと もうしますです
もうします already closes the sentence.
drills.why: もうす is the humble counterpart of いう, used about your own actions.

drills.q: Offer to carry your boss's bag.
drills.a: にもつを おもちします
w: にもつを もってあげます
てあげる sounds like you are doing them a favour from above.
にもつを おもちになります
That is the honorific form, which raises your own action.
にもつを おもちです
です does not work as a verb here.
drills.why: お plus stem plus する lowers your own action when it affects someone senior.

drills.q: Ask whether they know what time it starts.
drills.a: なんじに はじまるか しっていますか
w: なんじに はじまりますか しっていますか
The embedded question takes the short form.
なんじに はじまるか しりますか
Knowing something is しっています.
なんじに はじまるを しっていますか
An embedded question keeps か.
drills.why: A question inside a larger sentence keeps か and takes the short form.

grammar.b: A small set of verbs that lower you in formal settings: ございます, おります, いたします, まいります.
e: やまだと もうします。
My name is Yamada.

grammar.b: お + stem + する lowers your own action when it affects someone senior.
e: にもつを おもちします。
Let me carry your bag.

grammar.b: Doing one thing without doing another.
e: あさごはんを たべないで きました。
I came without eating breakfast.

grammar.b: A question tucked inside a bigger sentence: short form plus か, or かどうか when there is no question word.
e: なんじに はじまるか しっていますか。
Do you know what time it starts?

grammar.b: Introducing a name you do not expect the listener to know.
e: 「げんき」という きょうかしょです。
It is a textbook called Genki.

grammar.b: Attached to the ます-stem: easy to do, hard to do.
e: この ペンは かきやすいです。
This pen is easy to write with.

vocab: to be different, to be wrong

lessons.title: Burglar
lessons.sub: The passive, and things left in a state

drills.q: Say you had your wallet stolen by a thief.
drills.a: どろぼうに さいふを とられました
w: どろぼうが さいふを とられました
The person who did it takes に in a passive sentence.
どろぼうに さいふを とりました
That says you did the taking.
どろぼうに さいふを とられました です
ました already closes the sentence.
drills.why: In a passive sentence the affected person is the topic and the doer takes に.

drills.q: Say the window has been left open.
drills.a: まどが あけてあります
w: まどが あいています
That describes the state without implying anyone did it.
まどを あけてあります
With てある the thing takes が.
まどが あけておきます
ておく is doing something in advance.
drills.why: てある means someone did it on purpose and the result is still there.

drills.q: Say a burglar got in while you were out.
drills.a: るすの あいだに どろぼうが はいりました
w: るすの あいだで どろぼうが はいりました
あいだに is the set phrase for something happening within a span.
るすの あいだに どろぼうが はいっています
That describes a present state.
るすの あいだに どろぼうを はいりました
はいる does not take an object.
drills.why: あいだに marks something happening inside the span of something else.

grammar.b: る-verbs take られる, う-verbs change u to a plus れる (よむ → よまれる). The person affected becomes the topic and the doer takes に. Japanese often uses it where something unwelcome happened to you.
e: どろぼうに さいふを とられました。
I had my wallet stolen by a thief.

grammar.b: Something was done deliberately and the result is still there. Pairs with the transitive verb, unlike 〜ている with the intransitive.
e: まどが あけてあります。
The window has been left open.

grammar.b: "While" — something happens inside the span of something else.
e: るすの あいだに どろぼうが はいりました。
A burglar got in while I was out.

grammar.b: Where なる is "become", する is "make it become": make it bigger, quieter, cleaner.
e: へやを きれいに しました。
I made the room clean.

grammar.b: Wanting someone else to do something.
e: てつだってほしいです。
I want you to help me.

lessons.title: Education in Japan
lessons.sub: Making and letting people do things, and conditions

drills.q: Say the teacher made the students write an essay.
drills.a: せんせいは がくせいに さくぶんを かかせました
w: せんせいは がくせいを さくぶんを かかせました
A sentence cannot have two を.
せんせいは がくせいに さくぶんを かきました
That says the teacher did the writing.
せんせいは がくせいに さくぶんを かかれました
That is the passive, not the causative.
drills.why: かく becomes かかせる. With another object present, the person made to act takes に.

drills.q: Ask to be allowed to go.
drills.a: いかせてください
w: いってください
That asks someone else to go.
いかれてください
That is the passive.
いかせるください
It attaches to the te-form: いかせて.
drills.why: Causative te-form plus ください asks for permission: "please let me".

drills.q: Say that even though you studied a lot, you forgot it.
drills.a: たくさん べんきょうしたのに、わすれました
w: たくさん べんきょうしたので、わすれました
ので gives a reason, so this says studying caused it.
たくさん べんきょうしましたのに、わすれました
のに attaches to the short form.
たくさん べんきょうしたのに、わすれます
The result belongs in the past.
drills.why: のに marks a contrast that disappoints what you would expect.

grammar.b: "Make" or "let" someone do something. る-verbs take させる, う-verbs change u to a plus せる. Whether it is forcing or allowing depends on context and on the particle: を for making, に for letting.
e: せんせいは がくせいに さくぶんを かかせました。
The teacher made the students write an essay.

grammar.t: Causative + てあげる/てくれる/てもらう
grammar.b: Combines with the giving verbs to make permission explicit: let me do it, please let me do it.
e: いかせてください。
Please let me go.

grammar.b: A firm instruction from a parent or teacher. It appears constantly on exam papers.
e: はやく ねなさい。
Go to bed, now.

grammar.b: Another conditional, closer to pure "if" than たら. う-verbs change u to eば; る-verbs drop る and add れば.
e: あした あめが ふれば、いきません。
If it rains tomorrow, I will not go.

grammar.b: "Even though" — marks a contrast that disappoints expectations.
e: たくさん べんきょうしたのに、わすれました。
Even though I studied a lot, I forgot it.

grammar.b: "Like" — comparing one thing to another.
e: ゆめのような はなしです。
It is a story like a dream.

lessons.title: Good-bye
lessons.sub: Being made to do things, and deciding

drills.q: Say you were made to sing at the party.
drills.a: パーティーで うたわされました
w: パーティーで うたわせました
That means you made someone else sing.
パーティーで うたわれました
That is the plain passive.
パーティーで うたいさせられました
うたう becomes うたわせる, then うたわされる.
drills.why: Causative plus passive: you had no choice, and the reluctance is built into the form.

drills.q: Say you will go even if it rains.
drills.a: あめが ふっても いきます
w: あめが ふったら いきます
That is "if it rains, I will go", without the concession.
あめが ふるても いきます
ても attaches to the te-form: ふって.
あめが ふっても いきません
That says you will not go.
drills.why: te-form plus も means "even if".

drills.q: Say you have decided to go to Japan.
drills.a: にほんに いくことに しました
w: にほんに いくことに なりました
That means it was decided for you.
にほんに いくことを しました
The pattern uses に.
にほんに いったことに しました
With the past form it would be about experience.
drills.why: ことにする is your own decision; ことになる is a decision that came from elsewhere.

grammar.b: Being made to do something you did not want to do. Build the causative, then make it passive: のませる → のまされる. The feeling of reluctance is built in.
e: パーティーで うたわされました。
I was made to sing at the party.

grammar.b: "Even if". Take the te-form and add も.
e: あめが ふっても いきます。
I will go even if it rains.

grammar.b: Deciding to do something, as a one-off decision.
e: にほんに いくことに しました。
I have decided to go to Japan.

grammar.b: Something you have made a habit of, as a matter of policy.
e: まいあさ はしることに しています。
I make a point of running every morning.

grammar.b: "Until" — the point where something stops.
e: あめが やむまで まちます。
I will wait until the rain stops.

grammar.b: Attached to the ます-stem, it means "the way of doing": つかいかた, how to use.
e: この かんじの かきかたを おしえてください。
Please tell me how to write this kanji.

grammar.q: わたし＿＿ りゅうがくせいです。
grammar.why: は marks the topic — the thing the sentence is about.

grammar.q: これは わたし＿＿ かばんです。
grammar.why: の joins two nouns. わたしのかばん = my bag.

grammar.q: にくを たべます＿＿。
grammar.why: か at the end turns a statement into a question.

grammar.q: メアリーさんは アメリカじんです。ソラさん＿＿ かんこくじんです。
grammar.why: も = too. Use it instead of は when adding a second person or thing.

grammar.q: うち＿＿ おんがくを ききます。
grammar.why: で marks where an action happens.

grammar.q: がっこう＿＿ いきます。
grammar.why: に marks the destination. で would be where something happens instead.

grammar.q: コーヒー＿＿ のみます。
grammar.why: を marks the direct object — the thing the verb acts on.

grammar.q: この とけいは ごせんえんです＿＿。（right?）
grammar.why: ね asks the listener to agree — "right?".

grammar.q: あの とけいも はっせんえんです＿＿。（I tell you）
grammar.why: よ tells the listener something you are sure of and they may not know.

grammar.q: いぬじゃないです。ねこ＿＿。
grammar.why: Plain statement: です. じゃないです is the negative.

grammar.q: ソラさんは がくせい＿＿。（is not）
grammar.why: じゃないです is how Lesson 2 makes a noun sentence negative.

grammar.q: ＿＿は なんですか。（the thing in your own hand）
grammar.why: これ is near the speaker, それ near the listener, あれ far from both.

grammar.q: ＿＿は なんですか。（the thing the other person is holding）
grammar.why: それ is the one near the listener.

grammar.q: ＿＿ ほんは いくらですか。（that book, over by you）
grammar.why: この/その/あの go in front of a noun. これ/それ/あれ stand alone.

grammar.q: トイレは ＿＿ですか。
grammar.why: どこ asks where.

grammar.q: これは ＿＿ かばんですか。（whose）
grammar.why: だれの + noun asks whose something is.

grammar.q: せんこうは ＿＿ですか。
grammar.why: なん before です; なに before a particle or in なにじん.

grammar.q: いま ＿＿ですか。
grammar.why: なんじ asks the time.

grammar.q: ソラさんは ＿＿ですか。（what year at university）
grammar.why: なんねんせい asks which year of study.

grammar.q: たけしさんは ＿＿ですか。（how old）
grammar.why: なんさい asks age.

grammar.q: でんわばんごうは ＿＿ですか。
grammar.why: なんばん asks for a number such as a phone number.

grammar.q: この ぼうしは ＿＿ですか。（how much）
grammar.why: いくら asks a price.

grammar.q: やさいを ＿＿。（I do not eat）
grammar.why: ます becomes ません for the polite negative.

grammar.q: おさけを ＿＿。（I drink）
grammar.why: のむ is a う-verb: the む becomes み before ます.

grammar.q: まいにち べんきょう＿＿。
grammar.why: する is irregular: する → します.

grammar.q: あした がっこうに ＿＿。（I come）
grammar.why: くる is irregular: くる → きます.

grammar.q: テレビを ＿＿。（I watch）
grammar.why: みる is a る-verb: drop る, add ます.

grammar.q: ぜんぜん テレビを ＿＿。
grammar.why: ぜんぜん and あまり need a negative verb to finish the sentence.

grammar.q: You meet your teacher at 8 p.m. ＿＿
grammar.why: こんばんは once it is dark.

grammar.q: You are leaving the house. ＿＿
grammar.why: The one leaving says いってきます; the one staying answers いってらっしゃい.

grammar.q: You have just got home. ＿＿
grammar.why: ただいま on arriving home; おかえりなさい is the reply.

grammar.q: Before eating. ＿＿
grammar.why: いただきます before the meal, ごちそうさま after it.

grammar.q: A shopkeeper greets you with ＿＿
grammar.why: いらっしゃいませ is what the shop says as you come in.

grammar.q: You decide to buy it: この かばんを ＿＿。
grammar.why: （〜を）ください = please give me this one.

classes.idea: Japanese uses three sets of characters at once. You need two of them for this course.
body: This is the thing that puts people off before they start, so it is worth getting straight on day one. Japanese writes with three systems mixed together in the same sentence, and they are not alternatives — each does a different job.

Hiragana is the rounded one. It is the backbone: grammar, endings, and any Japanese word you do not write another way. Forty-six basic characters. This is where you start and it is what Lesson 1 drills.
Katakana is the angular one. Same sounds, different shapes, used for words borrowed from other languages — コーヒー, テレビ, ペン. Another forty-six, learned in Lesson 2.
Kanji are the Chinese characters, and there are thousands. They start in Lesson 3 and carry on for years. Your midterm does not test them and in fact forbids them: you write your answers in kana.
So the job in front of you is two alphabets of forty-six, not thousands of anything. Each character is one sound and the sound never changes, which is kinder than English.
shape: Chinese characters — later, and not on your midterm
ex: コーヒー is katakana because the word was borrowed; the rest is hiragana.
slips: Learning all three at once
Hiragana first, properly
Katakana arrives in Lesson 2 and kanji in Lesson 3. Taking them in order is the course design, not impatience.

check.q: Which system do you learn first, and which does your midterm forbid?
check.why: Hiragana is Lesson 1. The midterm says answers in Japanese, no kanji.

check.q: コーヒー is written in katakana because:
o: It is borrowed from another language
check.why: Katakana marks borrowed words.

classes.idea: English says who did what by the order of the words. Japanese says it by tagging each word.
body: In English, "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" use exactly the same words. The only thing telling you who bit whom is the order. Move a word and you change the meaning.

Japanese does not work that way. Each word carries a small tag — a particle — saying what job it is doing in the sentence. Because the job is written on the word itself, the order can move and the meaning does not. That is why a Japanese sentence can look scrambled to an English eye and still be perfectly clear.

So a particle is not decoration and it is not a preposition. It is a label saying: this word is the topic, this one is the thing being acted on, this one is where it happens. Learn the job each particle marks and the sentences stop being a word jumble.
One more thing worth knowing early: the verb goes at the end, always. Everything before it is labelled pieces in more or less any order.
shape: the topic — what the sentence is about
the thing the verb acts on
where you are heading, or a point in time
too, as well — it replaces は
turns the sentence into a question
ex: わたしはにくをたべます。
わたし is the topic, にく is the thing being eaten. Two different jobs, two different tags.
で because the eating happens there.
に because home is where you end up. Same word, different job, different particle.
の glues them: the second noun is the main thing, the first describes it.
そらさんもがくせいです。
も replaces は. You never write もは.
slips: がっこうでいきます。
がっこうにいきます。
いく needs a destination, not a venue. You are not doing something at the school, you are heading to it.
うちにたべます。
うちでたべます。
Eating is an action that happens somewhere, so で. に would mean you are travelling into the house.
わたしもはがくせいです。
わたしもがくせいです。
も takes the place of は. The two never sit together.
にくがたべます。
にくをたべます。
The meat is being eaten, so it is the object: を.

Because it cannot — the order is fixed
check.why: The job is tagged on the word, so the position is free. Only the verb is pinned, at the end.

classes.t: The marks that change a kana
classes.idea: A few small additions turn the basic kana into every other sound Japanese has.
body: Once you have the basic set, four small devices cover the rest, and all of them are written smaller or as marks beside the character.
Two strokes in the top right — dakuten — voice the consonant: か becomes が, さ becomes ざ, た becomes だ, は becomes ば. A small circle — handakuten — only goes on the は row and makes p: は becomes ぱ.
A small ゃゅょ after an i-row character squeezes two sounds into one beat: きゃ, しゅ, ちょ. Written full size they would be two beats, which is a different word.

A small っ doubles the consonant after it and is held as a beat of silence: ざっし is not ざし. And a long vowel just adds the vowel kana — おばあさん against おばさん — which in katakana is written with a bar instead: コーヒー.
The small ones are genuinely smaller on the page. Writing them full size changes the word.
shape: handakuten — only on は: は→ぱ
small — one beat with the kana before it
ex: Small ゅ — one beat, not two.
Katakana writes its long vowels with a bar.

じゅう
Full-size ゆ makes it two beats and a different word.
ざし
ざっし
Without the small っ the consonant is not doubled — and it is not a word.

check.why: Only は, making ぱぴぷぺぽ.

check.q: じゅう and じゆう differ how?
o: One is one beat, the other is two
check.why: The small ゅ joins the beat before it; full size is its own beat.

classes.idea: は does not mean "is". It announces what you are about to talk about.
body: は is usually explained as the subject marker. That is close enough to be useful and wrong often enough to trip you up. What it really does is set the topic: "as for X, ...".
So わたしはがくせいです is not quite "I am a student" — it is closer to "as for me, student". The です is doing the "is". は is only pointing at what the sentence concerns.
This matters because once a topic is set, Japanese drops it. If it is obvious you are talking about yourself, you do not keep saying わたしは. Sentences with no visible subject are normal, not lazy.
And one spelling oddity: as a particle it is written は but said "wa". Everywhere else は says "ha".
shape: As for X, it is Y.
ex: わたしはがくせいです。
せんこうはにほんごです。
Topic dropped, because it was already clear.
slips: わたしはがくせい。
わたしはがくせいです。
は does not mean "is". Without です the sentence has no verb.

check.q: は is written は but pronounced how, when it is a particle?
check.why: As a particle it is said "wa".

check.q: What does は actually do?
o: It marks the topic — what the sentence is about
It makes the sentence a question
check.why: It sets the topic. です does the work of "is".

classes.idea: の sticks two nouns together, and the last one is the thing you are really talking about.
body: English does this with apostrophes, "of", or just stacking words: my book, a student at VIU, Nanaimo, BC. Japanese uses one particle for all of it: の.
The order is the opposite of what English sometimes does. The describing noun goes first, the main noun goes last. わたしのほん — the ほん is the thing; わたし just says whose.
Once glued, the whole lump behaves like one noun, so you can drop it into a bigger sentence wherever a noun would go. And you can chain them: だいがくのせんせい — a university teacher.
shape: the B that belongs to / relates to A — B is the main thing
ex: A student, of the university kind.
たけしさんのせんこうはれきしです。
The glued lump たけしさんのせんこう is the topic of the sentence.
slips: ほんのわたし
わたしのほん
Back to front. The owner comes first, the thing comes last.

check.q: In AのB, which one is the main thing?
check.why: The last noun is the thing; what comes before it describes it.

check.q: How do you say "my teacher"?
check.why: Owner first, thing last.

classes.idea: Japanese does not reorder a sentence to ask a question. It adds one syllable at the end.
body: English flips the words around: "you are a student" becomes "are you a student?". Japanese leaves the sentence exactly as it is and puts か on the end.
That is the whole mechanism. がくせいです becomes がくせいですか. Your voice does not even have to rise — the か has already done the job.
The same か works with a question word in the sentence: せんこうはなんですか. English would move the "what" to the front; Japanese leaves it exactly where the answer would go.
ex: せんこうはなんですか。
The question word sits where the answer will sit, not at the front.
slips: かがくせいです。
がくせいですか。
か goes at the end, never the front. It is not "do" or "are".

check.q: How do you turn がくせいです into a question?
o: Move です to the front
Change です to ですかい
check.why: か on the end, nothing else moves.

check.q: Where does the question word go in せんこうはなんですか?
check.why: It sits in the answer’s place. Japanese does not move it forward.

classes.t: The question words, and the counters they attach to
classes.idea: なん means "what", and it fuses with a counter to ask "how many of that thing".
body: You already have なん and なに, which are the same word. なん goes before です and before a counter; なに goes before a particle. That is the only rule separating them.

The useful part is what happens when なん attaches to a counter. Japanese counts different things with different words — じ for hours, さい for years of age, ねんせい for school years, ばん for numbers. Stick なん on the front of one and you get the matching question.
So you are not learning five separate question words. You are learning one word and four counters, which you already know.
shape: なんねんせい — what year student
ex: でんわばんごうはなんばんですか。
としょかんはどこですか。
slips: なにですか。
なんですか。
Before です it is なん. なに comes before a particle instead.

check.q: How do you ask someone’s age?
check.why: さい is the age counter, so なんさい.

check.q: なん or なに before です?
check.why: なん before です and before a counter.

classes.t: こ・そ・あ・ど: two decisions, not twelve words
classes.idea: These twelve words are a grid. Pick how far away it is, then pick what shape the sentence needs.
body: Learners meet これ, この, ここ, それ, その, そこ and so on as a list of twelve things to memorise, and it is miserable. They are not twelve things. They are two choices.
First choice, the beginning of the word: こ is near me, そ is near you, あ is away from both of us, ど is the question — which one?
Second choice, the ending: れ stands alone and means "one", の goes in front of a noun, こ/そ/あそこ is a place. Put the two together and the word builds itself.

The one that catches people is これ against この. これ is already the noun — "this one". この cannot stand by itself and must have a noun after it. これはあ and このほん are both fine; この by itself is not a sentence.
shape: これ / それ / あれ / どれ
stands alone — this one, that one
この / その / あの / どの + noun
must be followed by a noun
ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ
a place — here, there, over there
ex: あのとけいはたかいです。
That watch over there is expensive.
あの because it is far from us both, and it has a noun after it.
A place, so the こ ending.
slips: これほんはたかいです。
このほんはたかいです。
これ cannot take a noun after it. Before a noun you need この.
このはなんですか。
これはなんですか。
この needs a noun. Standing alone, it has to be これ.

check.why: そ is near the listener.

check.q: Which one can stand on its own, with no noun after it?
check.why: これ is already "this one". この must be followed by a noun.

check.q: "The bank is over there."

check.why: A place, far from both of you: あそこ.

classes.idea: も means "as well", and it takes the place of は rather than joining it.
body: When you want to add a second person or thing to something already said, you swap は for も. Not add — swap.
たけしさんはにほんじんです。やましたせんせいもにほんじんです。 The second sentence does not need to repeat the whole idea; も carries "also is Japanese" on its own.
The reason it replaces は is that both are doing the same job — pointing at what the sentence is about. You cannot point twice.
ex: そらさんもがくせいです。
あのとけいもたかいです。
That watch over there is expensive too.
Works with anything, not just people.
slips: そらさんはもがくせいです。
そらさんもがくせいです。
も replaces は. The two never appear together.

o: そらさんはもがくせいです
そらさんもがくせいです
そらさんをもがくせいです
もそらさんがくせいです
check.why: も stands in for は.

classes.t: じゃないです: saying it is not
classes.idea: To make a noun sentence negative, swap です for じゃないです.
body: This is the whole of it. がくせいです becomes がくせいじゃないです. Nothing else in the sentence changes.

It is worth saying what this is not: it is not how you make a verb negative. たべます does not become たべますじゃないです — verbs have their own negative, ません, which Lesson 3 covers. じゃないです is only for sentences that end in です after a noun.
In answers it usually follows いいえ: いいえ、にほんじんじゃないです。
ex: がくせいじゃないです。
いいえ、にほんじんじゃないです。
The usual shape of a "no" answer.
slips: たべますじゃないです。
たべません。
じゃないです is for nouns. A verb goes negative with ません.

check.q: "I am not a student."
o: がくせいじゃないです
がくせいですじゃない
check.why: Noun sentence, so です becomes じゃないです.

check.q: How do you make たべます negative?
o: たべますじゃないです
check.why: Verbs use ません; じゃないです is only for nouns.

classes.t: ね and よ: checking and telling
classes.idea: Two syllables that say what you expect the listener to do with the sentence.
body: ね invites agreement. You already think it is true and you are checking, or you are being companionable: このコーヒーはおいしいですね — "this coffee is good, isn’t it".
よ goes the other way. It says: I know this and you probably do not. あのとけいもはっせんえんですよ — new information, handed over.
Neither is compulsory and both are easy to overuse. よ on something the other person obviously knows can sound like you are correcting them.
shape: I tell you — new to the listener
ex: このとけいはごせんえんですね。
slips: メアリーさんのせんこうはにほんごですよ。
メアリーさんのせんこうはにほんごですね。
Telling Mary her own major with よ is odd. She knows it; ね is the one that fits.

check.q: You want the other person to agree with you. Which?
check.why: ね seeks agreement.

check.q: You are telling them something they do not know. Which?
check.why: よ hands over new information.

classes.idea: Which group a verb is in is the whole of knowing how to conjugate it.
body: Japanese verbs fall into three groups, and the group decides what happens when you make the polite form. Learn the group with the verb and conjugation is automatic; learn the verb without it and you are guessing every time.
る-verbs are the easy ones: drop る, add ます. たべる becomes たべます.
う-verbs end in a consonant sound plus う. The last kana shifts to its i-row partner before ます: のむ becomes のみます, かく becomes かきます, はなす becomes はなします.
And two verbs are irregular: する becomes します, くる becomes きます. べんきょうする is just a noun stuck onto する, so it follows する.
The trap: かえる ends in る but is a う-verb. It is かえります, not かえます. Your exam likes this one.
shape: last kana moves to the i-row, add ます
する→します, くる→きます
ex: かえる → かえります
Looks like a る-verb, is not.
slips: かえます
かえります
かえる is a う-verb despite the る.
のむます
のみます
The む has to move to み first.

check.q: かえる is which group?
check.why: A う-verb that ends in る — hence かえります.

check.q: のむ in its polite form:
check.why: う-verb: む → み, then ます.

check.q: べんきょうする follows which pattern?
o: する, because it is a noun plus する
check.why: Noun + する, so べんきょうします.

classes.t: ます and ません: present and future, both at once
classes.idea: One form covers "I do" and "I will do". Context, not grammar, tells them apart.
body: The ます form is called present tense, which is slightly misleading. It covers habits — things you do regularly — and things you are going to do. It does not cover the past.
まいにちコーヒーをのみます is a habit. あしたコーヒーをのみます is tomorrow. Same verb form; the time word does the work.
The negative is ません, and it behaves the same way: たべません is both "I do not eat" and "I am not going to eat".
ex: まいにちコーヒーをのみます。
あしたがっこうにいきます。
I am going to school tomorrow.
slips: たべますじゃないです。
たべません。
じゃないです is for nouns. Verbs take ません.

check.q: あしたたべます means:
check.why: ます covers the future; あした says when.

check.q: The negative of のみます:
check.why: ます → ません.

classes.t: あまり and ぜんぜん need a negative
classes.idea: Two of the frequency words are only half a sentence until the verb goes negative.
body: Most of the frequency words are straightforward: よく often, ときどき sometimes, たいてい usually. They sit before the verb and that is that.
But あまり and ぜんぜん are different. あまり means "not much" and ぜんぜん means "not at all" — the "not" is part of their meaning, so the verb has to be negative as well. あまりたべます is not a sentence.
Think of them as needing a partner: the adverb sets up the negative and the verb delivers it.
shape: よく / ときどき / たいてい + ます
あまり / ぜんぜん + ません
ex: あまりテレビをみません。
I do not watch much TV.
ぜんぜんおさけをのみません。
I do not drink alcohol at all.
slips: ぜんぜんのみます。
ぜんぜんのみません。
ぜんぜん carries a "not" and needs the verb to agree.

check.q: あまりテレビをみ＿＿。
check.why: あまり needs a negative verb to finish it.

check.q: Which of these can finish with a positive verb?
check.why: よく is ordinary; the other two need ません.

classes.t: Numbers, and the three that change sound
classes.idea: Japanese numbers stack like building blocks, with a handful of sound changes you have to know.
body: Up to ten you simply learn them. After that they stack: 23 is にじゅうさん, literally two-ten-three. 45 is よんじゅうご. Hundreds and thousands work the same way.
Four and seven have two readings each — よん/し and なな/しち — and which one you use depends on what follows. For counting and for most counters, よん and なな are the safe ones.

The part that catches people out is the hundreds, where three numbers change sound: 300 is さんびゃく not さんひゃく, 600 is ろっぴゃく, and 800 is はっぴゃく. Those three are worth saying out loud until they are automatic, because they turn up in prices constantly.
ex: A small つ and a ぴ.
slips: さんひゃく
さんびゃく
300 takes a び.
ろくひゃく
ろっぴゃく
600 doubles the consonant and takes a ぴ.

check.why: Small つ and ぴ.
さんびゃく.

classes.t: Greetings, and the ones that come in pairs
classes.idea: Several greetings are halves of an exchange, and learning one without the other leaves you stuck.
body: The time-of-day ones are simple enough: おはようございます in the morning, こんにちは through the day, こんばんは once it is dark. Dropping ございます makes it casual, for friends and family.

The ones worth special attention are the pairs, because Japanese expects the other half. The person leaving says いってきます and the one staying answers いってらっしゃい. Coming home it is ただいま and おかえりなさい. Before eating いただきます, after it ごちそうさま.
Learn each pair as one unit. Half a pair is a question with no answer.
shape: いってきます ↔ いってらっしゃい
ただいま ↔ おかえりなさい
ex: Polite; drop ございます with friends.
Once it is dark — your exam asks this one.
slips: ごちそうさま。(before eating)
いただきます。
いただきます before, ごちそうさま after.

check.why: Dark, so こんばんは.

check.q: Someone says いってきます to you. You answer:
check.why: That is the other half of the pair.

topic: Who or what is this sentence about?
The topic comes first and takes は. It is the thing the rest of the sentence is about — usually the person doing it. は is written with the kana は but said wa.
object: What is the verb acting on?
The thing being eaten, read, watched, drunk. を and nothing else. If you can put "it" in the English — I eat IT — that word takes を.
place: Where does the action take place?
で marks the place an action happens: eating AT home, studying AT the library. Not に. に is for arriving somewhere, で is for doing something somewhere.
dest: いく, くる and かえる take a destination, and a destination takes に (or へ, which is also accepted). You are not doing something there, you are going there.
when: On what day or in what period?
A day or a dated period takes に: どようびに, しゅうまつに. The に may be dropped and the exam accepts it either way, but putting it in is never wrong.
time: あした, きょう, あさ, こんばん — times measured from now rather than named on a calendar. These take no particle at all. Adding に to あした is a mistake.
freq: まいにち, よく, ときどき, たいてい, まいばん. No particle. They sit after the topic and before the rest of the sentence.
deg: How much — and does it force a negative?
あまり and ぜんぜん take no particle and force the verb negative: あまり...ません, ぜんぜん...ません. Writing them with ます is wrong even though it reads fine.
manner: An い-adjective describing the verb drops い and takes く: はやい becomes はやく. No particle.
verb: The verb is always last. Put it in its polite form: ます, or ません when the English says not.

where: どこ asks where something IS. The answer is the place and です — nothing else needs to come back. そこ, あそこ and a named place are all fair answers.
what: なん／なに asks what something is. Give the thing and です. The question word is replaced by the answer; the rest of the sentence stays put.
who: だれ asks which person. Note it is not だれが here — だれ sits where the answer will sit.
whose: だれの asks whose. The answer keeps the の: ソラさんのぼうしです. Dropping the の turns "Sora’s hat" into "Sora, a hat".
price: いくら asks how much it costs. The answer is the number plus えん plus です. Watch the sound changes: ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく, さんぜん.
time: なんじ asks what time. ごぜん and ごご go in front of the hour, not behind it, and はん comes after it: ごぜんじゅうじはんです.
age: なんさい asks how old. Answer with the number plus さい. はたち is the one exception, at twenty.
year: なんねんせい asks which year of study. The answer is the number plus ねんせい — いちねんせい through よねんせい.
number: なんばん asks for a number, usually a phone number. Read the digits one at a time and say の where the dash would be.
yesno: はい、〜です。／いいえ、〜じゃないです。
A question with no question word in it is a yes-or-no question. Answer はい or いいえ, then give the same shape back — じゃないです for the negative, never ではありません on this paper.
yesnov: yes or no, with a verb
はい、〜ます。／いいえ、〜ません。
A verb question answers with the same verb: はい、のみます or いいえ、のみません. You do not repeat the whole sentence, only the verb.
whatdo: なにを asks what you do something to. The answer puts the thing where なに was, keeps the を, and keeps the verb.
wheredo: どこで asks where you do it. The place goes where どこ was, the で stays, and so does the verb. This is the one people answer with just a place — the verb has to come too.
